speaker: edwards

With regard to oral argument, we typically reserve five minutes rebuttal for the appellate if you'd like anything different, just tell us. And you can assume we're familiar with the facts and law as set forth in the record and in the briefs, but you may proceed, Mr. Appellant.

speaker: robertadams
text: Good morning, may it please the court. My name is Robert Adams. I am counsel for Appellant Mr. Ruiz. Your Honor, the case before you comes because appellant is asking the court to find that the trial court erred in denying Mr. Appellant's dispositive motion to suppress. The motion to suppress raised the issue of whether the plain smell or plain view of cannabis. In Mr. Ruiz's case, it was plain smell. Rape is sufficient on its own to constitute probable cause for a detention and search of his vehicle. The issue of cannabis providing probable cause has historically been that result by saying cannabis alone is probable cause. The smell of cannabis is unique. It is so telltale that an officer can easily identify it, whether it's in raw or burnt form and provides a distinct probable cause that the person is in possession of cannabis. However, that was at a time when the possession of cannabis was always categorically illegal. That is no longer the case. The Florida legislature has changed the cannabis laws. So to add the hemp program, which is statute 581.217, and to also add the medical use statute, statute 381.986, and specifically amended the medical use statute to include the ability to possess prescription cannabis in a form for smoking. These additions come also with a change to the definition of cannabis under the controlled substances, section 893.02, subsection 3, changing the definition of cannabis to specifically exclude cannabis that is in compliance with the medical use statute, meaning it's possessed, purchased, manufactured in compliance with that statute, or cannabis that qualifies as hemp under the definition in 581.217, section 2D that provides a definition of hemp as cannabis plant that contains a THC concentration of 0.3% or less. The changes to the definition, we can liken to the changes to the definition of concealed carry of a firearm, which was addressed by the first DCA and the Kilburn case, where the first DCA held that since the definition of the crime has changed to specifically state that the crime is committed when a person who does not have a concealed carry permit is possessing a firearm while concealed, that person has committed the crime. And the addition of that change to the definition, making it a requirement that the person not have the CCW license, meant that law enforcement needed something in addition to just seeing the gun that was tucked into Mr. Kilburn's waist to decide...
